source.title: Universal Stagewise Learning for Non-Convex Problems with Convergence on Averaged Solutions
source.authors: Zai-Yi Chen; Zhuo-Ning Yuan; Jin-Feng Yi; Bowen Zhou; En-Hong Chen; Tian-Bao Yang

record.file_problem: Text is full; figure labels contain garbled character encoding, but the main results and Table 1 are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own CIFAR-10/100 results comparing stagewise and baseline optimizers, including training and test error, and argues that some training recipes are less prone to overfitting. This refines optimizer-related generalization claims; it does not test random-label memorization or the other listed mechanisms.
record.gate_note: Only the ResNet-20 experiments directly compare training and test error for optimizer variants and explicit ℓ2 regularization. Table 1 reports final test errors; Figures 1–4 report training and test error curves but their plotted values are figure-only. Optimization convergence theorems and cited findings are not catalog rows.
record.test_reason: Table 1 directly compares held-out error of adaptive optimizers (AdaGrad and AMSGrad) with SGD and momentum methods on the same ResNet-20 workloads. These comparisons bear on V4, although the extracted rows emphasize improvements within optimizer families rather than the relevant comparisons between families.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the empirical conclusions: stagewise methods outperform theoretical variants and achieve similar or sometimes better test error than heuristic variants. The authors interpret usually lower heuristic training error as suggesting less overfitting with stagewise methods. They also report comparable performance among stagewise optimizers without a consistent winner. Their formal contribution concerns optimization convergence, not a generalization guarantee.
record.recipe_differences: Stagewise proximal optimization with averaged stage solutions; compared against iterative-decay theory variants and fixed-frequency-decay heuristic implementations.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and ℓ2 regularization setting change the reported test errors; the authors state the best stagewise method depends on dataset and whether regularization is added.

fits_no_version.finding: Stagewise optimization improves the test error of corresponding conventional optimizer implementations; heuristic implementations usually have lower training error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stagewise proximal optimization with averaged solutions can improve held-out performance relative to other implementations of the same optimizer.

record.problems: Experiments cover one architecture (ResNet-20) and two image datasets; reported table gives final test error only, while training and test error trajectories are figure-only. No uncertainty estimates or controls are reported. The comparison changes multiple recipe details and is not a controlled isolation of adaptive optimizers' generalization.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant numeric rows were omitted. Figures 1–4 contain separate training/test curves by optimizer, dataset, and regularization condition, but plotted values are figure-only and there are already tabled final test-error rows for each optimizer/dataset/regularization combination; figures 1–4 are summarized by the textual conclusion excerpts rather than reconstructed into extra rows.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label generalization.
Width sweeps and performance beyond interpolation.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.

Adam itself, language benchmarks, optimizer switching, decoupled weight decay, and a controlled broad-tuning comparison. Exact adaptive-versus-SGD training-performance comparisons cannot be recovered from the supplied figure text.
Batch-size comparisons and adaptations to large-batch training.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with other generalization measures.

missing.what: Dedicated heuristic adaptive-versus-nonadaptive comparisons. In column order CIFAR-10 with/without regularization, CIFAR-100 with/without: AdaGrad 10.71/13.80/37.04/41.06%; AMSGrad 10.76/11.13/38.62/39.96%; SGD 8.34/10.81/33.67/37.19%; SHB 8.58/10.28/33.30/37.56%; SNAG 8.85/10.34/33.89/36.84%. Existing baselines contain the numbers but do not encode these comparisons.

Dedicated theory-schedule comparisons. In the same column order, AdaGrad is 12.11/13.96/39.09/44.49%, versus SGD 16.25/19.18/43.51/45.78%, SHB 15.67/16.55/39.15/46.23%, and SNAG 17.64/16.76/39.34/44.21%. AdaGrad uses a constant learning-rate parameter; the nonadaptive methods use iterative inverse-square-root decay.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted Table 1 values are correct. Row states above use comparisons between stagewise adaptive and nonadaptive methods; their original within-family baselines answer a different question. All initial learning rates were tuned over the same five values, while stagewise methods additionally tuned proximal strength and stage length. These comparisons therefore do not isolate adaptivity from all recipe choices. Regularized runs use a coefficient of 5e-4. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Adam comparisons, language benchmarks, broad hyperparameter tuning, switching optimizers, and word-level language models.

relationships.condition: Heuristic AdaGrad and AMSGrad versus heuristic SGD and momentum methods; both datasets, with and without weight regularization.
relationships.reason: Table 1 shows both adaptive methods have higher test error than every heuristic nonadaptive comparator in all four settings; this verdict uses the table directly because these comparisons lack dedicated rows.
relationships.display_finding: Reported test error favored every heuristic nonadaptive comparator over AdaGrad and AMSGrad across the specified settings, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Stagewise methods on CIFAR-10 with and without regularization, and CIFAR-100 with regularization.
relationships.reason: Stagewise AdaGrad has higher test error than stagewise SGD, SHB and SNAG in each setting (R7 versus R1/R3/R5; R8 versus R2/R4/R6; R15 versus R9/R11/R13).
relationships.display_finding: Reported test error favored stagewise SGD, SHB, and SNAG over stagewise AdaGrad in the specified settings, but these comparisons remain unverified.

relationships.condition: Stagewise methods on CIFAR-100 without regularization.
relationships.reason: Adaptive performance depends on the comparator: AdaGrad's 34.62% beats SGD's 34.95%, nearly matches SHB's 34.49%, and trails SNAG's 33.29% (R16/R10/R12/R14).
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdaGrad error below SGD, near SHB, and above SNAG remains unverified.

relationships.condition: Theory-schedule AdaGrad versus theory-schedule SGD and momentum methods.
relationships.reason: Table 1 directly shows AdaGrad beating all three nonadaptive theory variants in three settings; on unregularized CIFAR-100 it beats SGD/SHB but trails SNAG, showing schedule-dependent rankings omitted as dedicated rows.
relationships.display_finding: Reported AdaGrad advantages over the nonadaptive theory-schedule variants remain unverified and do not extend to every setting.

reader_labels.condition: ResNet-20 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; with and without ℓ2 regularization
reader_labels.reason: The tested stagewise recipes generally yield lower final test error than the paper's theoretical and heuristic SGD, SHB, SNAG, and adaptive baselines, but the paper does not isolate adaptive-optimizer generalization under matched tuning; rows R1–R16 compare recipe-level outcomes.
